newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's political future on operating table.
newsitem.headline: Russia's political future on operating table.

text.p: The surgeons operating on President Boris Yeltsin on Tuesday had in their hands the fate of Russia's entire political leadership and the health of a system heavily dependent on the man at the top.

The 65-year-old president, who went under the surgeon's knife at 7 a.m. (0400 GMT), holds immense powers under Russia's constitution ranging from nominating the prime minister to control of the armed forces.

If the operation is successful and Yeltsin survives, it means the preservation of a political elite and policies which Western leaders and many investors still regard as the best guarantors of stability in the world's largest country.

His death or failure to recover fully would signal the start of a power struggle much fiercer than the rivalries already rocking the Kremlin and create the possibility of a major change in direction under a new leader.
"One thing we do not need is another election campaign now," said military and political analyst Alexander Konovalov.
"I look around at the potential presidential candidates and I see only figures from the past, no figures of the future."

Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin would stand in for Yeltsin for three months until a new election were held if the president, his ally, proved unable to govern. He would also be a likely presidential candidate.
Other challengers would include Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov, sacked national security adviser Alexander Lebed and probably Moscow Mayor Yuri Luzhkov.
"Chernomyrdin would probably have similar policies to Yeltsin but under Lebed, anything could happen," said Viktor Kremenyuk, deputy director of the USA and Canada Institute thinktank.

The election of the 52-year-old Zyuganov would prompt fears in the West. Luzhkov, 60, would also provoke uncertainty because although a familiar figure on Moscow's political scene, it is not clear what policies he would pursue as a national leader.
Another election would also be disastrously expensive -- not least in lavish election campaign promises -- and compound Russia's economic difficulties.
Yeltsin designed the 1993 constitution, narrowly approved in a nationwide referendum, specifically to suit himself.
His powers allow him to dominate the parliament and the government. He is commander-in-chief of the armed forces and has control of Russia's many nuclear weapons.
In short, he is the top of a pyramidic power structure in which all are answerable to him.
"The president is the main stabilising factor in the country," Luzhkov told Interfax news agency.
So far the system has held out in his absence and fears of an army or "palace" coup have proved unjustified, despite poltical infighting and discontent in the armed forces.

If Yeltsin does not make a full recovery, aides such as Chernomyrdin and Anatoly Chubais, the head of the Kremlin administration, would have an interest in trying to keep him in power as a figurehead leader for as long as possible.
Most analysts say the charismatic Lebed would be favourite to win an early election and that the dour Chernomyrdin needs time to brush up his image.

If Yeltsin were merely a figurehead, it would mean a continuation of the uncertainty that has increased since Yeltsin fell ill four months ago just before his reelection on July 3. It would give scope for Kremlin infighting to continue.

But even if Yeltsin makes a full recovery, stability is far from guaranteed. At 65, even after a successful heart operation, many politicians doubt Yeltsin still has the energy needed to keep the system fully under his control.
"Yeltsin will not come back as he once was," said political analyst Andrei Kortunov, head of the Russian Science Foundation.
"Even if the operation is successful, his age and general condition mean he will have to change his role and become the 'legitimiser', dealing with overall strategy rather than day-to-day governing."
One danger in all the scenarios is that the leaders' eyes remain fixed on keeping power rather than on solving the economic problems piling up while Yeltsin is out of the Kremlin.
An International Monetary Fund delegation left Moscow late last month without agreement to release the latest tranche of a $10-billion loan becasue of dismay over low tax revenues.
Protests on Tuesday by trade unions representing millions of workers who have not been paid for months illustrated the danger of leaving economic problems unsolved.

"Unless the government starts working as one body, we will lose what control we still have and we will plunge into complete and final chaos," Zyuganov has said. "The country is at the end of its tether."
